sections.title: Start here
sections.body:
Surveying turns measurements on the ground into positions, areas, volumes and elevations. Angles and distances give horizontal position. A level and a rod give height.

Most questions are careful bookkeeping: add and subtract in the right order and keep track of direction.
pitfalls: Swapping backsight and foresight. Backsight is added to the known elevation and foresight is subtracted.
Mixing bearings and azimuths without converting.

sections.title: Angles, distances and trigonometry
sections.body:
Surveying measures angles and distances and turns them into positions. Directions are written two ways. An azimuth is one angle from 0° to 360°, clockwise from north. A bearing is an angle up to 90° from north or south toward east or west, such as S 35° W.

Distances measured along a slope must be reduced to horizontal. The interior angles of a closed traverse with n sides should add to (n - 2) × 180°; the shortfall or excess is the misclosure and is spread among the angles.
pitfalls: Measuring a bearing from the east-west line. Bearings are always from north or south.

example.problem: Convert an azimuth of 200° to a bearing.
example.steps:
200° is 20° past south, on the west side.

Bearing = S 20° W.

sections.title: Area computations
sections.body:
Land area is computed from the coordinates of the corners or from measured offsets. The coordinate method cross-multiplies around the boundary and halves the result. For irregular boundaries, offsets measured at regular intervals are summed by the trapezoidal rule or Simpson's rule.

A triangle's area follows from two sides and the included angle, or from all three sides. Areas are often wanted in hectares (10,000 m^{2}) or acres (43,560 ft^{2}).
pitfalls: Listing the corners out of order around the boundary.
Forgetting to halve the cross-multiplied sum.

example.problem: Find the area of a triangle with corners at (0, 0), (40, 0) and (0, 30) metres.

sections.title: Earthwork and volume computations
sections.body:
Earthwork volume is found from cross-sections cut along the route. The average end area method multiplies the mean of two neighbouring cross-section areas by the distance between them. It slightly overestimates when the sections differ a lot. The prismoidal formula is more exact because it also uses the middle section.

For pits and building sites, a grid of cut depths gives volume as plan area times average depth. Soil swells when dug and shrinks when compacted, so bank, loose and compacted volumes differ.
pitfalls: Adding cut and fill together. Keep them separate.

example.problem: Stations 30 m apart have fill areas of 18 m^{2} and 26 m^{2}. Find the fill volume.

sections.title: Coordinate systems
sections.body:
Positions are recorded as northings and eastings on a plane grid, such as a state plane system, or as latitude and longitude on the curved earth. State plane coordinates flatten a zone of the earth so that ordinary plane geometry works within small errors.

Each traverse line has a latitude (its north-south part) and a departure (its east-west part). Add them to the coordinates of the starting point to get the next point. In a closed traverse the latitudes and the departures should each add to zero; what is left is the error of closure.
pitfalls: Swapping sine and cosine: with azimuths from north, cosine gives the north part.

example.problem: A line runs 150 m at an azimuth of 120°. Find its latitude and departure.
example.steps:
Latitude = 150 cos 120° = -75.0 m (south).

Departure = 150 sin 120° = 129.9 m (east).

sections.title: Leveling
sections.body:
Leveling finds elevations with a level and a graduated rod. The instrument gives a horizontal line of sight. A backsight on a point of known elevation gives the height of the instrument. A foresight on a new point is subtracted to give its elevation.

Carry elevations forward through turning points and close on a known benchmark to check the work. Grade is rise over run, usually as a percent.
pitfalls: Adding the foresight instead of subtracting it.

example.problem: From a benchmark at 50.00 m, the backsight is 2.10 m and the foresight on point A is 0.85 m. Find the elevation of A.
